slides.html: 1–2. SDF and HJ Bounds
slides.title: 1–2. SDF and HJ Bounds

slides.html:
Example: a two-state economy

m=(0.7,1.2), each with probability 1/2: E[m]=0.95, R_f=1.053.

A stock paying (2,\,0.5): price =1.0, E[R]=1.25, excess return 0.197.

Poor payoff in the bad state \Rightarrow risky \Rightarrow high expected return.
slides.title: Example: a two-state economy

slides.html:
The Pricing Equation

p=E[mx],\qquad 1=E[mR],\qquad R_f=\frac1{E[m]}
  • CRRA: m=\beta(C_{t+1}/C_t)^{-\gamma}
  • E[R]-R_f=-R_f\operatorname{cov}(m,R): premium ⇔ negative covariance with m
  • \dfrac{|E[R]-R_f|}{\sigma(R)}\le\dfrac{\sigma(m)}{E[m]}
slides.title: The Pricing Equation

slides.html:
Hansen–Jagannathan Bound

Project m on payoffs: m^\star=E[mx]'E[xx']^{-1}x; the residual is orthogonal, so

\operatorname{var}(m)=\operatorname{var}(m-m^\star)+\operatorname{var}(m^\star)\ge\operatorname{var}(m^\star)
\frac{\sigma(m)}{E[m]}\ge SR_{\max},\quad \operatorname{var}[m^\star(\nu)]=\nu^2(E[R]-\tfrac1\nu)'\Sigma^{-1}(E[R]-\tfrac1\nu)
slides.title: Hansen–Jagannathan Bound

slides.html: 3. GMM
slides.title: 3. GMM

slides.html:
GMM and the J Test

\hat\theta=\arg\min g_T'W_Tg_T,\qquad W=S^{-1}\ \text{optimal (two-stage)}
J=T\,g_T'\hat S^{-1}g_T\sim\chi^2_{M-K}
  • Hansen–Singleton (1982): large J, CRRA rejected
  • Mehra–Prescott (1985): exact identification, implausible \gamma
  • weak instruments: asymptotics unreliable
slides.title: GMM and the J Test

slides.html: 4. Equity Premium Puzzle
slides.title: 4. Equity Premium Puzzle

slides.html:
Resolutions

Idea Mechanism
recursive utility separate \gamma and EIS; estimates imply late resolution
long-run risk persistent expected growth enters the SDF
habit risk aversion \gamma/S_t rises in bad times
heterogeneity stockholders, uninsurable risk
disasters, measurement missing data or wrong consumption
slides.title: Resolutions

slides.html:
Habit and the Debate

U=E\sum\beta^j\frac{(C-X)^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma},\qquad S=\frac{C-X}{C}
  • matches premium and PD variation; effective risk aversion \approx100
  • long-run risk vs habit: R^2 of PD on lagged \Delta c
  • in habit data CAPM beats consumption models
slides.title: Habit and the Debate

slides.html: 5–6. Predictability
slides.title: 5–6. Predictability

slides.html:
Intuition: what a high price means

A high price/dividend ratio: either low future returns or high dividend growth.

Example: P/D=1/(r-g): r=8\%\to7\% lifts P/D from 20 to 25.
slides.title: Intuition: what a high price means

slides.html:
Present-Value Identity

r_{t+1}\approx\kappa+\rho(p-d)_{t+1}+\Delta d_{t+1}-(p-d)_t
p_t-d_t=\text{const}+E_t\sum\rho^{j-1}(\Delta d_{t+j}-r_{t+j})

High PD ⇒ high future dividend growth, low future returns, or both.
slides.title: Present-Value Identity

slides.html:
Return Decomposition

\eta=\eta_d-\eta_r: dividend news minus discount-rate news.

VAR z_{t+1}=Az_t+w: \ \eta_r=e_1'\rho A(I-\rho A)^{-1}w

Campbell: 1927–51 dividend news; 1952–88 return news; about half of the variance explained.
slides.title: Return Decomposition

slides.html:
Joint Tests, WLS, Out-of-Sample

  • Cochrane (2008): b_r=1-\rho\phi+b_d; b_d\approx0 ⇒ returns predictable
  • Johnson (2019): WLS ≈ 25% less volatile than OLS
  • Goyal–Welch: out-of-sample R^2 can be negative
slides.title: Joint Tests, WLS, Out-of-Sample

slides.html:
Evidence: Stocks

  • PD, payout yield, net payout yield, book-to-market, spreads, variance risk premium
  • in-sample strong, out-of-sample fragile
  • fixes: economic restrictions, Bayesian methods
slides.title: Evidence: Stocks

slides.html:
Evidence: Bonds and Currencies

Test EH slope
\Delta y on yield spread 1
excess return on yield spread 0
excess return on forward–spot spread 0

Campbell (1995) rejects EH; Cochrane–Piazzesi: one forward-rate factor \gamma'f, loadings b^{(N)}. UIP: slope <1 — forward premium puzzle.
slides.title: Evidence: Bonds and Currencies

slides.html: 7–8. Factor Models
slides.title: 7–8. Factor Models

slides.html:
Intuition: risk premium = exposure \times price

E[R]=R_f+\sum_k\beta_k\lambda_k

Example: 2\%+1.1\times6\%+0.5\times2\%=9.6\%.
slides.title: Intuition: risk premium = exposure \times price

slides.html:
Conditional Models

Managed portfolios R_{t+1}z_t; a_t=a_0+a_1x_t gives factors x_t,f_t,x_tf_t.

Hansen–Richard: conditional ⇒ unconditional is possible, not the reverse; instruments z_t must be used.
slides.title: Conditional Models

slides.html:
Evidence and Facts

value · momentum · short-term reversal · post-earnings drift

Fama–French: market, SMB, HML — high R^2, but \alpha=0 still rejected.

Lettau–Ludvigson: conditional consumption CAPM fits the 25 portfolios much better.
slides.title: Evidence and Facts

slides.html:
The Critiques

  • Lewellen–Nagel: factor zoo; a_t,b_t linked by theory
  • Lewellen–Nagel–Shanken: with 25 size–value portfolios any factor with \operatorname{cov}(P,f)\ne0 can reach R^2\approx100\%

Fixes: more test-asset dimensions; impose theory (zero-beta = T-bill, \lambda = factor mean); report small-sample intervals.
slides.title: The Critiques

Intuition: what pure luck looks like

1000 managers flipping coins: at the one-sided 5% level about 50 "significantly outperform".

So look at the whole distribution, not just the best few.

slides.html: 10–11. Liquidity and Behaviour
slides.title: 10–11. Liquidity and Behaviour

slides.html:
Liquidity

  • market vs funding liquidity
  • Amihud ILLIQ=\frac1N\sum|R|/V positively related to returns
  • on-the-run vs off-the-run; repo specialness
  • Pástor–Stambaugh: liquidity beta; Acharya–Pedersen: three covariances
  • funding liquidity: leverage procyclical (Adrian–Shin)
slides.title: Liquidity

slides.html:
Who Is the Marginal Investor?

  • Mankiw–Zeldes: stockholders' consumption correlates with returns
  • Aït-Sahalia–Parker–Yogo: luxuries
  • Brunnermeier–Nagel: no clear wealth effect on risk aversion
  • Malmendier–Nagel: experience matters (\lambda>1)
  • Odean, Grinblatt–Keloharju: overtrading, disposition effect
slides.title: Who Is the Marginal Investor?

slides.html:
Review

Every model restricts m. High in-sample fit is not evidence: check bias, out-of-sample performance and test assets; with weak tests use more assets, theory and small-sample inference.
slides.title: Review

slides.html:
Common misconceptions

Misconception Correct
The puzzle is just too little data A deep conflict between \gamma and smooth consumption
A small R^2 means unpredictable 5%–10% annually matters for long horizons
In-sample significance makes money Check out of sample and bias correction
More factors are better Overfitting: the "factor zoo"
The best manager has skill Many land on top by luck
slides.title: Common misconceptions
